kurz: Why hardly any trading signals can be derived from highly predictable population trends, and where they affect your own financial planning.

bloecke.md:
Demographics is the part of macroeconomics that can be projected most reliably. The 55-year-olds of 2040 are 41 years old today and already live in Germany. Life tables change only slowly, and birth numbers affect the labour market only with a delay of two decades. The only variable that can fluctuate strongly in the short term is immigration.

For investors, this reliability has a drawback. What is almost certain is also known to almost everyone and has therefore long been reflected in prices, interest rates and property prices. Demographics is therefore of no use as a buy signal. It is suitable as a framework for decisions that have an effect over decades anyway, such as the savings rate, pension expectations, the choice of location for property and the expected burden of taxes and social contributions.

## Breaking down growth

All effects of demographics on an economy run through two channels, namely the number of people who work and the amount each of them produces in a year. This breakdown is rough, but it is well suited to testing statements about long-term growth.

bloecke.formel: GDP growth ≈ growth in the number of persons employed + growth in productivity per person employed
bloecke.erklaerung: Over long periods, economic growth is the sum of the growth in the number of persons employed and the growth in output per person employed. In the short term, the business cycle, working hours and capacity utilisation mask this relationship, but not over ten years or more.
variablen: number of people in work, driven by cohort size, labour force participation, retirement age and immigration
real value added per person employed, driven by capital stock, technology, organisation and skills
bloecke.beispiel: If the number of persons employed shrinks by 0.4% a year and productivity rises by 1.0%, the economy grows by around 0.6%. If the population stays the same, GDP per capita also grows by only around 0.6%, even though output per person employed rises by 1.0%. The gap arises because a smaller share of the population is working.

bloecke.titel: Growth contributions with a shrinking working population
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with plausible orders of magnitude; real GDP only grows if the productivity gain more than offsets the negative contribution of the falling headcount.

bloecke.md: Two things follow from this. First, a shrinking working population does not automatically lead to falling prosperity, because what counts for living standards is GDP per capita, not the number of persons employed. GDP per capita does, however, grow more slowly than output per person employed as long as the share of persons employed in the population is falling. Second, growth then depends entirely on productivity, the second term of the sum. In economic terms, the demographics debate is therefore about productivity. Most of the discussion is nevertheless about immigration, because people are easier to count than value added.

## Baby boom cohorts of 1955 to 1969 in Germany

The largest birth cohorts date from the late 1950s and the 1960s. In the record year of 1964, around 1.36 million children were born; in 2025 the figure was around 654,000. The total fertility rate in 2025 was around 1.32 children per woman, while the replacement level is 2.1. The fertility rate has been below this level for more than fifty years.

By the mid-2030s, a numerically large block of cohorts will therefore retire, while a much smaller one follows. Depending on the immigration assumption, the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) puts the decline in the working-age population by then at an order of magnitude of between just over three and just under five million people. The range is not due to measurement errors. It results from the different assumptions about immigration.

Europe as a whole is developing similarly, only with a time lag. Italy and Spain are further along, while France and Scandinavia are ageing more slowly because of higher fertility rates. China is ageing faster than any large country before it. Its population has been shrinking since the early 2020s, and the number of people of working age for just over a decade. Its fertility rate is even lower than Germany's. Unlike Japan or Germany, China is ageing at a per capita income at which these two countries still had a young population.

Japan's working population peaked in the mid-1990s. Since then, Japanese GDP has barely grown. Value added per person employed, by contrast, developed much as in many European countries. Portraying Japan as a disaster therefore confuses the total with the average. Conversely, social security systems and property markets depend on the total and on the age distribution, not on the average.

## Ageing and the level of interest rates

According to the widespread thesis, ageing lowers interest rates. People save mainly in the second half of their working lives. If particularly large cohorts are in this phase at the same time, a large supply of capital meets investment demand that tends to fall as the workforce shrinks. As a result, the price of capital falls. Together with the global savings glut described by Ben Bernanke, this is regarded as the standard explanation for why the [[natural rate of interest]] has fallen over decades.

Charles Goodhart and Manoj Pradhan argue the opposite. According to their reasoning, pensioners dissave, that is, they run down savings instead of building up new ones. They demand health and care services, which are labour-intensive and difficult to automate, and no longer produce anything themselves. If the number of consumers rises relative to the number of producers, labour becomes scarce. The consequences are rising wages, higher inflation and a higher interest rate. From the same demographic development, the two authors therefore derive the opposite effect on interest rates.

The data so far do not allow a decision between the two theses. The natural rate of interest cannot be observed. It is a model variable with wide error bands, and the two camps reach different results with different assumptions. The interest rate series also calls for caution. Germany's population aged continuously between 1990 and 2026, whereas the yield on ten-year Bunds moved in both directions.

bloecke.titel: Yield on ten-year Bunds from 1990 to 2026
bloecke.unter: Annual values; the point for 2026 is the daily value of 18 September 2026, not an annual average. Over these 36 years, the demographic trend ran continuously in the same direction, but interest rates did not.

bloecke.md:
## Pay-as-you-go financing of the statutory pension

In the statutory pension system, the block of cohorts has an effect without delay, because the system is financed on a pay-as-you-go basis (Umlageverfahren). The contributions of a year are paid out as pensions in the same year. In mid-2025, around 21.5 million people received a pension. In 2025, the federal government contributed around €98 billion to the pension insurance, the largest single item in the federal budget.

The adjustment formula of Section 68 SGB VI (Social Code Book VI, pension insurance) links pensions to wages. The [[sustainability factor (Nachhaltigkeitsfaktor)]], which reflects the ratio of pensioners to contributors, dampens the adjustment. The 48% floor (Haltelinie) for the pre-tax safeguard level (Sicherungsniveau vor Steuern) suspends this dampening until 2031. If the formula produces a lower level, the pension value is raised accordingly. Pensions are then not held back. Under Section 291b SGB VI, the federal government reimburses the pension insurance for the additional costs from tax revenue. The contribution rate, which under Section 158 SGB VI is derived from the level of the sustainability reserve (Nachhaltigkeitsrücklage), rises nonetheless, because expenditure grows faster than contribution income as the number of pensioners increases. Section 154(3) SGB VI obliges the federal government to propose measures to the legislature if, in the medium variant of the projection in the pension insurance report (Rentenversicherungsbericht), the contribution rate rises above 22% by 2030.

bloecke.titel: Contribution rate to the general pension insurance
bloecke.unter: Actual value for 2026 and illustrative calculation from the 2025 pension insurance report; the step in 2028 is necessary because the sustainability reserve would otherwise fall below its statutory minimum. The federal government reimburses the additional costs of the floor from tax revenue.

referenz.text: 22% review threshold under Section 154(3) SGB VI

bloecke.titel: Contribution rate and safeguard level according to the 2025 pension insurance report
A contribution rate 2.6 percentage points higher
bloecke.md:
Assume a gross monthly salary of €4,500, that is, below the contribution assessment ceiling (Beitragsbemessungsgrenze). If the contribution rate rises from 18.6% to 21.2%, the employee's share rises from 9.3% to 10.6%.

- Before: 4,500 × 9.3% = €418.50 a month
- After: 4,500 × 10.6% = €477.00 a month
- Difference: €58.50 a month, €702 a year

The employer pays the same amount on top. In economic terms, the employee usually bears this share as well, because gross wages turn out correspondingly lower. Together this comes to around €1,400 a year. With a savings rate of 10% of gross income, that is €5,400, just over a quarter of the capacity to save privately is lost. This shows what demographics means financially for someone who is 35 today.

## Migration and labour force participation

The number of births can hardly be steered by policy and only has an effect after twenty years. The standard retirement age is already rising to 67 and applies in full from the 1964 cohort onwards. That leaves immigration as the only variable that can change by six-figure numbers of people within a few years.

In economic terms, what counts is age and labour force participation, not the headcount. A person who takes up a job subject to social security contributions at the age of 28 is a net contributor over their lifetime. Without access to the labour market, the same person is a burden on the social security funds and public budgets. For public finances, the employment rate is therefore decisive. Estimates of the net migration at which the working population would remain stable are in the order of several hundred thousand people a year. The exact figure depends so heavily on the assumptions about the participation rate and retirement age that any point estimate suggests a precision that does not exist.

## Consequences for the property market

Homes are demanded by households, not by individuals. Because the average household size has been falling for decades, the number of households can still grow while the population is already shrinking. Demand for housing only falls when both numbers decline.

In addition, there are large regional differences. The population decline hits structurally weak rural districts first, not the major cities. A national average is therefore useless for a purchase decision. What is meaningful is net migration, age structure and the supply of jobs in the district concerned.

The third consequence is an increase in inheritances. The block of cohorts now retiring owns the largest part of Germany's property wealth. Estimates of the wealth inherited each year are in the order of several hundred billion euros. The inheritance tax statistics only record taxable cases and therefore systematically understate the volume. What matters for the tax are the allowances under Section 16 ErbStG (Inheritance and Gift Tax Act). They amount to €500,000 for spouses and €400,000 per child and can be used again every ten years, with Section 14 ErbStG adding together earlier gifts within this period. When an inherited property is sold, the ten-year period under Section 23 EStG (Income Tax Act) continues to apply, so the period that began with the deceased continues to run for the heir. For your own planning, it also matters when you inherit. This typically happens between the ages of 50 and 65. That does not help buyers who are in their early thirties today.

## The long-term debt cycle

Ray Dalio distinguishes between two cycles. The short-term cycle lasts around five to ten years and is steered by the central bank through the interest rate. It passes through the phases of upswing, overheating, rate rise, downturn and rate cut. The long-term cycle arises because each short-term cycle typically ends with a slightly higher level of debt than the previous one. At some point, debt service grows faster than income. Rate cuts then have no effect, because the interest rate is already at its lower bound.

In this situation, only four ways remain: saving and cutting spending, letting debts default or restructuring them, redistributing from the top down through taxes, or creating money and thereby devaluing the debts in real terms. Dalio calls a mix of these ways that avoids a severe crisis a “beautiful deleveraging”. Demographics acts here like an additional, unreported debt. Pension and long-term care commitments are not legally government debt and do not appear in the Maastricht ratio. In Germany, this ratio stood at 63.5% of GDP in 2025 and is likely to rise to around 66% in 2026. In economic terms, however, the commitments are promises of payment to a growing group.

The framework is an interpretive pattern and not a model that predicts timing. It shows which questions you should ask, for example who holds the debt, in which currency and at what interest rate. When something will happen cannot be derived from it.

bloecke.titel: Four channels through which ageing works
bloecke.unter: Only the third channel has an immediate effect according to fixed rules; for the other three, the direction or pace is disputed.

knoten.titel: More older people, fewer in work

bloecke.md: The most expensive mistake is to conclude from a reliable projection that a return is certain. Ageing has been known about for decades and is reflected in prices. At most, a deviation from it would be tradable, but that cannot be predicted. Investors who avoid German shares because of Germany's ageing population also overlook the fact that DAX companies generate most of their revenue outside Germany. A country's demographics therefore says little about the shares listed there.

Demographics does not change the question of whether to invest. It changes three variables in your own planning. The savings rate has to be set higher, because the contribution rate is rising and the safeguard level falls arithmetically after 2031. When buying property, location becomes more important than price. Your own retirement age is the variable with which you can influence the outcome most strongly.

bloecke.titel: The ratio of contributors to pensioners
bloecke.md:
Three ratios are regularly confused.

The **old-age dependency ratio** is a purely demographic ratio. It gives the number of people aged 67 and over per 100 people aged 20 to 66. It says nothing about who works and who pays contributions.

The pension insurance's **pensioner ratio** (Rentnerquotient) sets equivalent pensioners in relation to equivalent contributors. Both variables are standardised to average values, because part-time workers and small pensions would otherwise be weighted incorrectly. The pensioner ratio feeds into the sustainability factor of Section 68 SGB VI.

Finally, the number of pensions is higher than the number of pensioners, because one person can receive several pensions, for example an old-age pension and a widow's pension. If these variables are mixed up, the result is ratios that differ by double-digit percentages.

mitnehmen: Over long periods, growth is the sum of the growth in the number of persons employed and the growth in productivity per person employed; if the number of persons employed shrinks, productivity has to deliver all of the growth.

Whether ageing lowers or raises interest rates is unresolved, because the savings glut and dissaving work in opposite directions and the interest rate series since 1990 clearly supports neither of the two schools.

In the pay-as-you-go system, demographics has an effect without delay; the 48% floor applies until 2031, and for 2039 the illustrative calculation in the 2025 pension insurance report shows a contribution rate of 21.2% and a safeguard level of 46.3%.
For property, what counts is the number of households and the development of the region concerned, not Germany's population as a whole.
The known demographic development is already reflected in prices; it belongs in financial planning, not in the purchase decision of a single year.

begriffe.text: Number of people aged 67 and over per 100 people aged 20 to 66. The ratio is purely demographic and says nothing about how many of these people pay contributions.

Component of the pension adjustment formula under Section 68 SGB VI. It dampens the pension adjustment when the ratio of equivalent pensioners to equivalent contributors rises. Until 2031, it is overridden by the 48% floor (Haltelinie).

The real interest rate at which an economy is neither overheating nor operating below capacity, also called r-star. It cannot be observed and can only be estimated using models, so the error bands are correspondingly wide.

Situation in which planned saving persistently exceeds planned investment. Ben Bernanke described it as a global savings glut; it is regarded as one of the standard explanations for the long-term decline in interest rates.

Pattern described by Ray Dalio that spans several decades. The level of debt rises over several short interest rate cycles until debt service grows faster than income. After that, the remaining ways out are austerity, default, redistribution and money creation.
